title: Antibacterial Therapy & Stewardship: Cultures, Selection, Monitoring and Resistance Prevention
html:
Antibacterial therapy is safest when the right drug reaches the right suspected or confirmed bacterial target, at an effective exposure, for an appropriate duration, while the team actively limits toxicity, superinfection, and resistance. The RN connects bedside findings with microbiology, medication timing, organ function, administration safety, response, and the daily question: does this client still need this antibiotic, and is it still the best choice?

Learning goals

  • Distinguish prophylactic, empiric, and targeted antibacterial therapy.
  • Collect high-quality cultures without delaying emergency treatment.
  • Interpret culture and susceptibility reports in clinical context.
  • Recognize immediate allergy, infusion reaction, organ toxicity, and superinfection.
  • Apply drug-class safeguards without relying on memorized lists alone.
  • Support timely review, de-escalation, route change, and appropriate duration.
  • Teach clients to use antibiotics safely and avoid sharing or saving doses.

Start with indication and urgency

Prophylaxis prevents infection during a defined risk period, such as a procedure. Empiric therapy begins before the organism is fully identified and is guided by infection site, severity, likely pathogens, local resistance patterns, allergies, recent antibiotics, exposures, and client factors. Targeted therapy narrows or changes treatment after diagnostic information and clinical response clarify the likely cause.

Antibiotics treat susceptible bacteria, not viruses. Fever or an abnormal urinalysis alone does not prove bacterial infection. At the same time, suspected sepsis or another life-threatening infection requires urgent recognition, cultures and diagnostics when feasible, and prompt prescribed therapy. Do not create a harmful delay while pursuing a perfect specimen.

Obtain the right specimen at the right time

When ordered and clinically feasible, obtain appropriate cultures before the first antibiotic dose because treatment can reduce organism recovery. Use correct site preparation, container, volume, number of sets, labeling, and transport requirements. Avoid collecting from contaminated sites or existing devices unless specifically indicated.

A poor specimen can produce misleading results and unnecessary therapy. For blood cultures, use meticulous skin antisepsis and the ordered number and volume of sets. For urine, assess symptoms and use the specified clean-catch or catheter sampling method; never obtain a culture from a drainage bag. For respiratory samples, distinguish true lower-respiratory material from saliva when possible.

Culture first when feasible—not at the cost of rescue
In a stable client, collect ordered cultures before therapy. In a rapidly deteriorating client, coordinate specimen collection and antibiotic administration in parallel so diagnostics do not cause dangerous delay.

Read microbiology as evidence, not an automatic prescription

A preliminary Gram stain can guide early thinking but does not establish the final organism or susceptibility. A culture may represent infection, colonization, or contamination. Interpret it with the source, collection quality, symptoms, examination, imaging, inflammatory and organ-function trends, device status, and response.

Susceptibility categories such as susceptible, intermediate or susceptible with increased exposure, and resistant depend on laboratory standards and achievable drug exposure. “Susceptible” does not guarantee clinical success if the drug does not reach the infection site, source control is absent, the dose is inappropriate, or the result reflects colonization rather than the cause.

Report critical or newly actionable results promptly and document closed-loop communication. New culture data should trigger review of spectrum, dose, route, duration, allergy information, and whether therapy can be narrowed or stopped.

Assess before every dose

Verify the indication, infection site, current order, last dose, culture status, allergy and reaction history, pregnancy or lactation considerations when relevant, age and weight, renal and hepatic function, hydration, blood counts, interacting medications, vascular access, and required drug levels or other monitoring.

“Penicillin allergy” is incomplete. Ask what drug was taken, what happened, how soon, how severe it was, how long ago, and whether related drugs were tolerated later. Differentiate intolerance such as isolated nausea from immediate hypersensitivity such as hives, bronchospasm, angioedema, or anaphylaxis, and from severe delayed reactions involving skin or organs. Do not independently remove an allergy label; document details and use the approved evaluation pathway.

Time-dependent and concentration-dependent concepts

Some antibiotics work best when free drug concentration remains above the organism's susceptibility threshold for sufficient time; others depend more on achieving an adequate peak relative to the organism or on total exposure. These concepts explain why interval, infusion duration, renal clearance, and drug-level timing matter.

The RN follows the prescribed regimen and pharmacy guidance rather than independently altering timing. Protect scheduled intervals, investigate missed or delayed doses, verify extended-infusion instructions, and record actual administration time so laboratory levels and therapeutic decisions can be interpreted correctly.

Beta-lactams: allergy, dose interval and neurologic risk

Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and related beta-lactams disrupt bacterial cell-wall synthesis. Monitor for immediate hypersensitivity during and after administration, but also recognize delayed rash, cytopenias, diarrhea, kidney injury, and neurologic toxicity—especially with high exposure or impaired renal clearance.

If anaphylaxis is suspected, stop the suspected drug, assess airway, breathing and circulation, call emergency help, and follow the anaphylaxis protocol. A mild nonprogressive rash without instability still requires assessment and notification; do not automatically label every rash as anaphylaxis or continue without evaluation.

Vancomycin: exposure, kidney function and infusion reaction

IV vancomycin dosing and monitoring depend on indication, body size, renal function, changing clinical status, and institutional pharmacokinetic practice. Obtain drug levels at the specified time and document infusion and sampling times accurately. Rising creatinine, reduced urine output, excessive exposure, or concurrent nephrotoxins warrants prompt review.

A vancomycin infusion reaction may include flushing, erythema, itching, and sometimes hypotension during or soon after rapid infusion. Stop or slow the infusion as directed, assess severity and airway, notify the appropriate clinician, and follow the prescribed response. Do not assume all flushing is IgE-mediated allergy, and do not assume it is harmless when hypotension or airway symptoms are present.

Aminoglycosides: kidney, hearing and level timing

Aminoglycosides can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, and neuromuscular blockade is possible. Assess renal function, urine output, hydration, hearing or vestibular symptoms, concurrent nephrotoxins, and ordered serum concentrations. Drug-level interpretation depends on the exact dose and sample time; a mislabeled or mistimed level can lead to an unsafe change.

Report tinnitus, hearing change, vertigo, imbalance, rising creatinine, falling urine output, or unexpected weakness. Toxicity may not be fully reversible, so early recognition matters.

Other class-specific hazards

  • Fluoroquinolones: monitor for tendon pain or rupture, peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system effects, dysglycemia, QT-related risk, and aortic-risk warnings in susceptible clients. Separate administration from interacting multivalent cations when prescribed guidance requires it.
  • Macrolides: assess QT-prolonging combinations, electrolyte abnormalities, hepatic concerns, and interactions.
  • Tetracyclines: follow administration instructions for food, water, posture, cations, photosensitivity, and pregnancy or age considerations specific to the agent.
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: assess sulfonamide reaction history, renal function, potassium, blood counts, rash, and interactions.
  • Clindamycin and broad-spectrum agents: remain alert for significant antibiotic-associated diarrhea and C. difficile infection.
  • Linezolid: monitor blood counts with prolonged treatment, serotonergic interactions, neuropathy risk, and dietary or drug instructions as ordered.
  • Metronidazole: review neurologic and hepatic risks, interactions, and current product-specific alcohol guidance rather than relying on slogans.

These are cue categories, not complete prescribing instructions. Always use the current label, medication reference, pharmacy guidance, and client-specific order.

Differentiate allergy, infusion reaction and expected adverse effects

Immediate hives, facial or tongue swelling, wheezing, stridor, respiratory distress, hypotension, or collapse suggests anaphylaxis and demands emergency action. Local vein irritation, predictable gastrointestinal effects, and rate-related infusion reactions require different responses. Stop the suspected exposure when indicated, assess the whole client, preserve airway and circulation, and communicate precise timing and findings.

Do not use vague charting such as “allergic.” Record the drug, dose, route, time, onset, objective findings, interventions, and response. Accurate characterization protects future treatment choices.

Watch for C. difficile and other superinfection

Antibiotics disrupt normal flora and can permit overgrowth of resistant or opportunistic organisms. New clinically significant diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, ileus, or toxic appearance during or after antibiotics requires assessment and appropriate precautions and testing per policy. Do not give an antidiarrheal automatically before the cause and safety are evaluated.

Oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis, new resistant infection, or device-related infection may also emerge. Monitor beyond the original infection and continue hand hygiene and transmission-based precautions as indicated.

Antibiotic stewardship happens at the bedside

Stewardship seeks the best clinical outcome while minimizing avoidable toxicity, C. difficile infection, and resistance. Nursing contributions include documenting the indication and start time, collecting quality specimens, administering on schedule, recording allergy details, monitoring response and toxicity, reporting microbiology promptly, and prompting an antibiotic review when new data arrive.

Daily review may support narrowing spectrum, discontinuing duplicate or unnecessary coverage, changing IV to oral therapy when clinically appropriate, adjusting for organ function, confirming source control, and defining a stop date. De-escalation is not undertreatment when it is based on better evidence.

Teach for safe use

Explain the drug's purpose, schedule, administration instructions, important interactions, common effects, red flags, and follow-up. Clients should not share antibiotics, save leftovers, take someone else's prescription, or demand antibiotics for viral illness. Teach the client to follow the current prescription and contact the care team for missed doses, vomiting, inability to take medication, severe diarrhea, rash, breathing difficulty, neurologic symptoms, or other specified concerns.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify infection syndrome and severity, specimen quality, microbiology, allergies, prior antibiotics, organ function, interactions, access, dose timing, response, and toxicity.
  2. Analyze cues: Decide whether findings support infection, colonization, contamination, treatment failure, inadequate source control, adverse reaction, or superinfection.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Sepsis, anaphylaxis, airway compromise, severe drug toxicity, rapidly progressive skin reaction, and fulminant C. difficile outrank routine scheduling concerns.
  4. Generate solutions: Coordinate cultures and urgent therapy, clarify allergy details, consult pharmacy, protect dose timing, plan monitoring, and request evidence-based review.
  5. Take action: Administer safely, stop a dangerous exposure, support ABCs, report critical results, use appropriate precautions, and document actual times and responses.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Trend symptoms, vital signs, infection source, cultures, blood counts, renal and hepatic function, drug levels, adverse effects, route, spectrum, and duration.

Clinical example

A stable client is receiving broad empiric therapy for suspected pneumonia. Before the first dose, ordered blood and respiratory cultures were collected without delaying treatment. Two days later, the respiratory specimen identifies a susceptible organism, blood cultures remain negative, oxygen need and fever are improving, and renal function is stable. The RN reports the finalized result, confirms the actual dose and culture times, and prompts the scheduled antibiotic review. The team narrows therapy and defines a duration. The RN updates teaching and continues to monitor respiratory status, diarrhea, rash, renal function, and clinical response.

Original educational synthesis. Antibacterial selection, dosing, monitoring, drug levels, allergy evaluation, duration, and infection-control actions require the current prescription, microbiology data, product labeling, pharmacy and stewardship resources, organizational policy, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official NCSBN product.
